svg.text: For plants and single cells, depth is the instrument.

a class sampled both ways gives the same depth profile by each
how deep a class is recorded, against how often it was sequenced
each mark is one class; both axes are shares of that class's records
share of the class's records that are DNA sequencing runs
Rank correlation between the two axes is +0.97 across the thirteen classes
sampled from water, and +0.73 with forams added back. Forams are the
exception that names the mechanism: 2.2% sequencing but 39.6% below 50 m,
because their largest dataset is the Deep Sea Drilling Project. No line is
fitted — the statistic is a rank correlation and a straight line would claim
each class's records across sea surface temperature, coldest-centred first
°C at the surface · tick is each class's mean
Sorted by mean, not mode: six classes peak at 10° and six more at
20°, so a modal ordering would tie them. Seagrasses are the warmest
class in the file at 21.5° and the only one with no weight at all
below 5°, which is a tropical and subtropical plant showing through
a register that is otherwise North Atlantic. Cryptophytes are the
OBIS v3 statistics/env and /dataset with a taxon filter, fetched 2026-09-18. Sequencing share is a keyword match on the titles of each class's 100
largest datasets (16S, 18S, metagenome, amplicon, eDNA, metabarcoding, Tara Oceans, Australian Microbiome), which cover 93–99% of every class's
records; it is a method label read off a title, not a field OBIS publishes. Every class was checked against /v3/taxon for rank Class and status
accepted, because OBIS resolves unaccepted synonyms silently — Fragilariophyceae and Bacillariophyceae return an identical 6,389,742 records.
